items.prompt: What happens to your heartbeat when you run fast?

options.why: Your heart never stops while you exercise. It works harder.
Your muscles need more oxygen, so your heart beats faster, not slower.
Running makes your heart work harder, so the beat changes.

hints: Put your hand on your chest after running.
Your muscles need more blood when they work hard.
Think about how your heartbeat feels after a race.
items.explanation: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen and food. Your heart beats faster to pump more blood to them.

items.prompt: Choose 3 habits that help keep you healthy.

options.why: Children need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep to grow and learn.

options.text: drinking sweet drinks instead of water
options.why: Water is the best everyday drink. Sweet drinks are for sometimes.

hints: Think about sleep, exercise and keeping clean.
Cross out habits that could make you tired or harm your teeth.
Look for the three habits a doctor would praise.
items.explanation: Washing hands removes germs, active play makes your heart and muscles stronger and good sleep helps you grow. Late nights and lots of sweet drinks do not help.

items.prompt: Why should you wash your hands with soap before eating?

options.why: Soap does not change the taste of food.
Washing cleans hands. It does not make them stronger.

options.text: Soap helps wash away germs that can make you ill.

options.why: Water helps, but soap removes many more germs.

hints: Think about tiny living things you cannot see.
Your hands touch many things during the day.
What does soap remove from your skin?
items.explanation: Your hands pick up germs from things you touch. Soap and water wash the germs away, so they do not get into your food.

items.prompt: The chart shows Tono's pulse after different activities. How many more beats per minute after running than resting?

figure.alt: Bar chart of pulse in beats per minute: resting 80, walking 95, skipping 120, running 140.

hints: Find the bar for running and the bar for resting.
How many more means find the difference.
Take the resting number away from the running number.
items.explanation: Running gave 140 beats per minute and resting gave 80. 140 take away 80 is 60.

items.prompt: How many hours of sleep do most 8-year-olds need each night?

options.why: That is far too little. Your body grows and rests while you sleep.
That is still too little for a child.
That is about how much a newborn baby sleeps.

hints: Children need more sleep than adults.
Adults need about 7 to 9 hours.
Think about going to bed at 8 p.m. and waking at 6 a.m.
items.explanation: Children aged 6 to 12 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. Sleep helps the body grow and the brain learn.

items.prompt: After playing football in the hot sun, what is the best drink?

options.why: Sugary drinks have lots of sugar. Water is best for replacing lost water.
You lose water when you sweat. You need to drink soon.
Sea water is far too salty and makes you thirstier.

hints: Your body loses water when you sweat.
Think about the healthiest way to put that water back.
Choose the drink with nothing added.
items.explanation: When you sweat, your body loses water. Plain water puts it back without extra sugar.

items.prompt: Lina finds some tablets in a drawer. What should she do?

options.text: Leave them and tell a trusted adult.
Take one to see what it does.
options.why: Medicines can harm you if they are not meant for you.
Medicine should only be given by a trusted adult, like a parent or doctor.

options.text: Hide them in her school bag.
options.why: Hiding medicine is not safe. A trusted adult should know.

hints: Medicines can help, but they can also harm.
Think about who should decide if someone takes medicine.
What is the safest thing a child can do?
items.explanation: Medicines are only safe when a trusted adult, like a parent or doctor, gives them. Never take tablets you find.

items.prompt: Why do you breathe faster when you exercise?

options.why: Your lungs do not shrink. You breathe faster to take in more oxygen.
The air is the same. Your body needs more oxygen.

options.text: Your body needs to cool your feet.
options.why: Breathing faster is about oxygen, not cooling your feet.

hints: Breathing brings air into your lungs.
Air contains a gas your muscles use.
What do working muscles need more of?
items.explanation: Working muscles need more oxygen. You breathe faster and deeper to take in more oxygen from the air.

items.prompt: Bagus needs to sneeze. What is the best thing to do?

options.text: Sneeze into his hands and keep playing.
options.why: Germs stay on hands and spread to things he touches.
This spreads germs to the friend.

options.text: Sneeze into a tissue or his elbow, then wash his hands.
Hold the sneeze in for an hour.
options.why: Nobody can hold a sneeze for that long.

hints: Sneezes spray tiny drops that carry germs.
Think about how to catch the drops.
What should you do with your hands afterwards?
items.explanation: A tissue or elbow catches the tiny drops from a sneeze. Washing hands afterwards stops germs spreading.

items.prompt: Put the steps for washing your hands in order.
items: Rub soap all over your hands.
Dry your hands with a clean towel.
hints: You need water before soap can lather.
Think about what comes right before drying.
Start with wet hands.
items.explanation: Wet your hands, add soap and scrub for about 20 seconds. Then rinse and dry them with a clean towel.

items.prompt: Tono measures his pulse before, just after and 5 minutes after running. What do his results show?

head: When
Pulse (beats per minute)
figure.alt: Table of Tono's pulse: before running 80, just after running 140, 5 minutes later 95 beats per minute.

options.text: Exercise makes the pulse stay high all day.
options.why: After 5 minutes it had already dropped to 95.
His pulse went up from 80 to 140 when he ran.

options.text: The pulse is highest when resting.
options.why: Resting gave the lowest pulse, 80.

options.text: The pulse rises with exercise, then slowly falls back.

hints: Read the three numbers in order.
What happened to the pulse during running?
What happened during the 5 minutes of rest?
items.explanation: Tono's pulse went up from 80 to 140 when he ran. After resting it fell to 95, on its way back to normal.

items.prompt: After the same race, Ari's pulse is back to normal in 2 minutes. Budi's takes 6 minutes. What might this tell us?

options.text: Ari's heart may be fitter from regular exercise.

options.why: They ran the same race.

options.text: Budi's heart is stronger because it works longer.
options.why: A fitter heart usually recovers faster, not slower.

options.text: Pulse has nothing to do with fitness.
options.why: How fast the pulse recovers is one sign of a fit heart.

hints: Both boys ran the same race.
Regular exercise trains the heart.
Which heart got back to normal more quickly?
items.explanation: A fitter heart usually returns to its resting rate more quickly. Regular exercise helps the heart get fitter.
